title: The Way of Knowledge
intro: 97 days through chapters 13 to 18 of the Bhagavad Gita, from the field and its knower to the Gita's final verse.

posts.caption: This plan walks through chapters 13 to 18, the last third of the Gita. Many teachers sum up its three sets of six chapters as action, devotion and knowledge. Here Arjuna asks the questions behind this final part: what is prakriti, matter, and what is purusha, spirit; what is the field and who knows it. In plain terms, he is asking what we are made of, and what in us is aware.

Krishna answers with an image: the body is the kshetra, the field, and whatever knows it is the kshetrajna, the knower of the field. Shankara and others explain the name: the results of a person's actions ripen in the body as crops do in a field. The point is that the self who is aware is distinct from the body it knows. In many editions Arjuna's question is left out or unnumbered, so this verse is 13:1.

Asked what wisdom is, Krishna gives not a doctrine but a list of qualities that runs over five verses, starting with humility and including ahimsa, non-harming. The list ends by calling all of it knowledge, so jnana here means a way of living, not just information.

posts.display: Dispassion towards the objects of the senses, and also absence of egoism, insight into the pain and evil of birth, death, old age and sickness.
posts.caption: Krishna's list of what counts as true knowledge continues: vairagya, dispassion toward the objects of the senses, freedom from ego, and a clear view of the suffering in birth, death, old age and sickness. The point is not gloom but honesty: seeing life's limits plainly turns a person toward what lasts. In the Buddha's story, too, meeting old age, sickness and death helped set the young prince on his search.

Krishna turns to what is to be known: Brahman, the ultimate reality, which Besant renders "the Eternal." Knowing it, he says, brings immortality. Commentators explain that it is called neither being nor non-being because ordinary categories cannot capture it.

posts.display: Everywhere That hath hands and feet, everywhere eyes, heads, and mouths; all-hearing, He dwelleth in the world, enveloping all.
posts.caption: A vivid picture of Brahman present everywhere, with hands, feet, eyes and ears in every direction. The point is that ultimate reality is not far off: Shankara explains that it works through every hand and sees through every eye, because it is present in all beings. The line closely matches a verse of the Shvetashvatara Upanishad (3.16), one of many places where the Gita draws on the Upanishads. In many editions this is 13:13.

Brahman is described through paradox: outside and inside all beings, unmoving and moving, too subtle to perceive, far away and near. The paradoxes say that ultimate reality cannot be pinned to one place or quality. Commentators add that it is near to those who know it and far from those who do not. The Isha Upanishad uses the same pairs: it is far and it is near, within all this and outside all this.

Krishna uses two terms from Sankhya, one of India's oldest schools of philosophy: prakriti, matter or nature, and purusha, spirit or consciousness. Both, he says, are without beginning. Everything that changes, including body and mind, belongs to prakriti, and so do the gunas, the three qualities explored in the next chapter. The point is that the conscious self is not the part of us that changes.

Krishna promises that whoever truly knows purusha and prakriti, spirit and matter with its gunas, will not be born again, whatever their condition in life. Here freedom from samsara, the cycle of rebirth, comes through understanding. In many editions this verse is 13:23.

One of the chapter's best-known verses, numbered 13:27 in many editions. The supreme Lord dwells equally in all beings, deathless among the dying, and Krishna says that only one who sees this truly sees. The point is that real vision looks past bodies that perish to what does not. Advaita reads it as the one Self in all; theistic schools read it as God present within every distinct being.

In the Sankhya picture the chapter has been using, all action is carried out by prakriti, nature, working through body, mind and senses, while the Self is the witness and does not act. Krishna says that whoever sees this truly sees. The point connects with chapter 3: it is the ego's claim "I am the doer" that binds a person, and seeing through it brings freedom. Chapter 18 returns to the theme.

When someone sees the many different beings as resting in the One and unfolding from it, Krishna says, they reach Brahman, the Eternal. Seeing the many within the One is a central theme of the Upanishads, which the Gita draws on throughout. In many editions this verse is 13:30.
posts.display: When he perceiveth the diversified existence of beings as rooted in One, and spreading forth from it, then he reacheth the Eternal.

posts.caption: Krishna explains how the Self can live in a body without being changed by it. Space holds everything, yet nothing stains it; in the same way, the Self dwells throughout the body, untouched by what the body does or suffers. Besant's "ether" translates akasha, space, which Indian philosophy counts as the subtlest of the five elements.

As one sun lights the whole world, the knower of the field lights up the whole field. Consciousness is pictured as light that makes body and mind known without being changed by them. The chapter ends one verse later; its traditional title, Kshetra-Kshetrajna-Vibhaga Yoga, means the yoga of telling the field from its knower.

Chapter 14 explores the three gunas, the qualities of nature that Krishna says shape every mind and every thing. Its traditional title, Gunatraya-Vibhaga Yoga, means the yoga of distinguishing the three gunas. Krishna opens by calling this the highest knowledge, the one by which sages reached supreme perfection. The point is that understanding what drives us is itself a path to freedom.

Krishna describes creation in the language of birth. Commentators take "the great Eternal" (mahad brahma) here to mean prakriti, nature, the womb of all beings, with Krishna as the father who gives the seed. The point is that every creature, in whatever form it is born, shares the same divine parent.

Krishna names the three gunas: sattva, rajas and tamas. Besant calls them Harmony, Motion and Inertia; others say goodness, passion and ignorance. All three arise from nature, and all three tie the imperishable self to the body. The rest of the chapter asks how these forces hold a person, and how to get free of them.

Rajas is the guna of passion and activity: the restless drive that keeps a person always wanting and always busy. Krishna ties it to craving and attachment, and says it binds the self through attachment to action and its results. The Sanskrit for thirst here, trishna, is the word Buddhism uses, as tanha in Pali, for the craving that causes suffering.

Tamas, the third guna, is darkness or inertia. Krishna says it is born of ignorance and binds through carelessness, laziness and sleep. Its mark is less wickedness than dullness, a clouding of the mind so that what is real is not seen.

Krishna sums up the three bonds: sattva, which Besant calls Harmony, ties a person to happiness; rajas, Motion, ties to action; and tamas, Inertia, veils wisdom and ties to carelessness. Even sattva, the clear and luminous guna, still binds. The chapter's goal is to go beyond all three.

The gunas are always shifting. Now sattva overpowers the other two, now rajas, now tamas. In the Gita's psychology every person carries all three, and their changing balance shapes moods, choices and character.

Krishna gives the signs of each guna. When the light of knowledge shines through all the gates of the body, the senses and mind, sattva is growing. The next verses describe rising rajas as greed and restlessness, and rising tamas as darkness and delusion.

Those established in sattva rise upward, those of rajas stay in the middle, and those of tamas sink downward. Many commentators read this as where each leads after death: to higher worlds, back to human life, or to lower births. Besant's Harmony, Active and Inert stand for the three gunas.

Going beyond the three gunas is the chapter's goal, called being gunatita. The embodied self that crosses them is freed from birth, death, old age and sorrow. The word for the nectar of immortality, amrita, literally means "undying."

posts.display: Balanced in pleasure and pain, self-reliant, to whom a lump of earth, a rock and gold are alike, the same to loved and unloved, firm, the same in censure and in praise.
posts.caption: Arjuna has asked how to recognize someone who has gone beyond the gunas. Krishna's portrait: steady in pleasure and pain, seeing a clod of earth, a stone and gold as equal, the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, toward blame and praise. The portrait concludes in the next verse.

The portrait ends: the same in honor and disgrace, the same to friend and foe, letting go of every undertaking, often read as ventures driven by desire for results. Such a person, Krishna says, is gunatita, gone beyond the gunas.

The chapter ends with Krishna as the ground of Brahman, of immortality, of eternal dharma and of perfect bliss. The verse before names bhakti, unwavering devotion, as a way across the gunas. Advaita reads the "I" here as the Self that is Brahman; Gaudiya Vaishnavas read it as Krishna, source of the impersonal Brahman.

Chapter 15 opens with a famous image: the ashvattha, the sacred fig, as an upside-down tree with roots above and branches below. It stands for samsara, the world of repeated birth, rooted above in the divine and spreading downward into the world. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns, and Krishna says whoever understands this tree understands the Veda. The image goes back to the Katha Upanishad.

After the image of the upside-down tree, Krishna says it must be cut down with the firm weapon of non-attachment. Here he describes those who reach the imperishable goal beyond it: free of pride and delusion, past attachment, living in the Self, desire stilled, and freed from the pairs of opposites, pleasure and pain.

A key verse on the individual self, described as an eternal portion of Krishna. Schools read "portion" differently. Advaita teachers often compare it to space that only seems divided by a jar; Ramanuja and Madhva see the self as a real, eternally distinct part of the divine.

Krishna is describing the individual self, the jiva, which he calls an eternal portion of himself. It moves from body to body taking the mind and senses along, as the wind carries scent from flowers, and through them it experiences the world. Besant's capitalized "He" refers to this embodied self.

The self is present when it leaves a body, when it stays, and when it experiences the world through the gunas, yet the deluded do not notice it (Besant's "Him"). Those with the eye of knowledge, jnana-chakshus, do. The same phrase closed chapter 13.

Krishna describes his presence in the living world: entering the earth, he upholds all beings with his energy, and as soma, full of sap, he nourishes every plant. Soma was the sacred drink of Vedic ritual and is also a name of the moon, which many commentators say feeds plants with its sap.

Krishna says he is Vaishvanara, the digestive fire in living bodies, working with the breaths to digest four kinds of food. Commentators list them as food that is chewed, swallowed, licked and sucked. Many chant this verse as a prayer before meals, often after 4:24.

Krishna dwells in every heart, the source of memory and knowledge, and also of their loss. He is what all the Vedas seek to know, the maker of Vedanta, and the knower of the Vedas. Vedanta, "the end of the Veda," refers to the Upanishads and the philosophy built on them.

Krishna sets up the chapter's last teaching by naming two kinds of being (purusha): the kshara, perishable, which is all beings, and the akshara, imperishable and unchanging. Besant calls them Energies. Commentators differ on the imperishable: Shankara takes it as maya, the seed of the world, Ramanuja as the liberated self. Either way, the next two verses reveal something higher than both.

Beyond both the perishable and the imperishable is the highest purusha, Purushottama, "the supreme Person." Krishna says he is known by this name in the world and in the Veda. The name gives the chapter its traditional title, Purushottama Yoga.

Krishna calls this the most secret teaching, and says whoever understands it becomes wise and has done all there is to do. At twenty verses, chapter 15 is one of the Gita's shortest, yet it gathers the world, the self and God into a single picture.

posts.display: The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, cleanness of life, steadfastness in the Yoga of wisdom, almsgiving, self-restraint and sacrifice and study of the Scriptures, austerity and straightforwardness.
posts.caption: Chapter 16 contrasts two kinds of character, the daivi (divine) and the asuri (demonic). The point, as the chapter goes on to say, is that character shapes destiny: one set of qualities leads toward freedom, the other toward bondage. The divine list begins here with fearlessness and purity of heart and runs over three verses, including tapas, disciplined effort, and svadhyaya, study of the scriptures.

posts.display: Harmlessness, truth, absence of wrath, renunciation, peacefulness, absence of crookedness, compassion to living beings, uncovetousness, mildness, modesty, absence of fickleness.
posts.caption: The divine list continues with ahimsa (non-harming), truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, peace, compassion for living beings, gentleness and modesty. Many of these echo the yamas, the ethical restraints of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, which begin with ahimsa and truth.

The list ends with vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, and freedom from malice and pride. These, Krishna says, belong to one born to the divine nature. The word for these properties is sampad, wealth or endowment, so the chapter speaks of divine and demonic riches.

Now the opposite list, the asuri sampad or demonic qualities: hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance. In Hindu scripture the asuras are the rivals of the devas, the gods. Here the terms describe human character.

Divine qualities lead to liberation, demonic ones to bondage. Then Krishna turns to Arjuna directly and tells him not to grieve, for he is born with the divine qualities. After a long list, it is a moment of personal reassurance.

The description of the asuric nature begins. Such people, Krishna says, understand neither pravritti nor nivritti, when to act and when to refrain, and lack purity, good conduct and truth. Pravritti and nivritti, outgoing action and withdrawal, are two classic paths in Hindu thought.

The asuric worldview in its own words: the universe has no truth, no foundation and no God, and arises from desire alone. The Gita presents this as a view of life built on desire, from which the conduct described in the coming verses follows.

Bound by a hundred ties of expectation and given to desire and anger, such people pile up wealth by unjust means to feed their cravings. The Sanskrit asha-pasha means the noose of hope or expectation: a picture of people held captive by what they want.

Krishna describes where the arrogant, self-centered outlook he has been portraying leads: scattered among countless thoughts, caught in moha-jala, the net of delusion, absorbed in pleasure, falling into a foul hell. Hindu texts usually describe naraka, hell, as a place of suffering between births rather than an eternal state.

Driven by ego, power, pride, desire and anger, such people end up hostile to the divine. Since the Gita teaches that God dwells in every body, Krishna says their contempt for others, and even for themselves, is contempt for him. Chapter 13 described the same Lord seated in all beings.

Krishna says that whoever casts aside the guidance of scripture and lives as desire dictates reaches neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal. Besant's promptings of desire translates kama-kara, acting at desire's command. The chapter's last verse turns this into a positive rule.

The chapter closes by naming shastra, scripture, as the guide to what should and should not be done. The verse before contrasts this with acting on impulse and desire. Arjuna's question at the start of the next chapter grows directly out of this verse.

Chapter 17 opens with a question that follows from the end of chapter 16. If people worship with faith but outside the rules of scripture, Arjuna asks, where do they stand: in sattva, rajas or tamas? Besant renders the three gunas here as Purity, Passion and Darkness.

Arjuna has asked about people who worship with faith but outside the scriptures' rules. Krishna answers that shraddha, faith, takes the shape of each person's nature, and that a person is made of their faith. It is an often-quoted line on how belief and character are bound together.

Faith shows in what people worship. Those ruled by sattva worship the devas, the gods; those of rajas, yakshas and rakshasas, powerful spirits and demons; those of tamas, pretas and bhutas, ghosts and spirits of the dead. The chapter sorts much of religious life by the three gunas.

Krishna applies the three gunas to everyday life, starting with food. The point is that what people eat both reflects and shapes their inner state. Sattvic food, preferred by those of a pure nature, increases life, strength, health, joy and good cheer, and is savory, nourishing and agreeable. This passage is often cited as a source for the idea of a sattvic diet in yoga and Ayurvedic circles today.

Rajasic food is described as bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and burning, the kind that brings pain, grief and sickness. The list suggests excess and overstimulation, in keeping with rajas, the guna of restless activity.

Tamasic food is stale, tasteless, spoiled, left over or impure. Where sattvic food builds life and rajasic food overstimulates, tamasic food dulls, like tamas itself. Next, Krishna turns the same threefold lens on sacrifice.

Yajna, sacrifice or worship, is sattvic when offered as a duty for its own sake, as scripture directs, with no desire for reward. It echoes the core teaching of chapters 2 and 3: action done without attachment to its fruit.

Sacrifice is rajasic when performed for the sake of a reward, or for show. The same outward ritual can fall under different gunas depending on motive. Throughout this chapter, the inner attitude matters as much as the act.

Krishna broadens the idea of tapas, austerity, beyond physical hardship to discipline of body, speech and mind. Austerity of speech means words that cause no distress and are truthful, pleasant and beneficial, along with regular recitation of scripture. The point is that how one speaks is itself a spiritual practice. It recalls a well-known Sanskrit saying: speak what is true, speak what is pleasant.

Austerity of the mind: serenity, gentleness, silence, self-control and purity of heart. Silence, mauna, is placed under the mind rather than speech, as an inner stillness. With austerity of body and of speech, it completes the Gita's threefold tapas.

Austerity done to win respect, honor and reverence, or for display, is rajasic, and Krishna calls it unstable and fleeting. The next verse says austerity done in delusion, through self-torture or to harm another, is tamasic.

Dana, giving, is sattvic when given simply because giving is right, to someone who cannot repay, at the proper place and time, to a worthy person. It is a classic statement of giving without expecting a return.

Giving is rajasic when it expects something back, aims at a reward, or is done grudgingly. The next verse calls giving tamasic when it is careless or contemptuous, offered at the wrong place and time to the unworthy.

Near the chapter's end, Krishna explains Om Tat Sat, a threefold name of Brahman, the ultimate reality. Those who teach Brahman begin every sacrifice, gift and austerity by sounding Om, the sacred syllable. The point is that an act opened with Om is offered to the highest, not done for oneself. Many Hindu prayers and rituals still open with it.

Sat, the last word of the sacred phrase Om Tat Sat, means being and reality, and also goodness; Krishna adds that it names any praiseworthy act. The word lives on in satsang, the company of the good, and in sat-chit-ananda, being, consciousness and bliss. Many editions open each chapter's closing colophon with Om Tat Sat.

The chapter ends with the opposite of sat. Offering, giving or austerity done without shraddha, faith, is called asat, unreal, and bears no fruit in this life or the next. The chapter closes where it began, with faith.

Chapter 18, the last and longest at 78 verses, gathers the Gita's teaching together. Arjuna asks about two kinds of letting go: sannyasa, renunciation, and tyaga, relinquishment. Behind it lies the question he has carried since chapter 2: does a spiritual life mean withdrawing from action, or acting in a new way? He calls Krishna Hrishikesha, lord of the senses, and Keshinishudana, slayer of the demon Keshi.

Krishna distinguishes the two. Sannyasa, the sages say, is giving up actions done from desire; tyaga is giving up the fruit of all actions. Much of the chapter builds on tyaga, which lets a person keep acting in the world while letting go of attachment to results.

Some thinkers say all action should be dropped as a flaw; others say sacrifice, giving and austerity must be kept. Krishna sides with keeping them, calling them purifiers of the wise. The next verse adds that even these should be done without attachment to their fruit.

Relinquishment has three kinds too. It is sattvic when a required action is done simply because it ought to be done, without attachment or desire for its fruit. Abandoning duty out of confusion is tamasic, and abandoning it to avoid hardship is rajasic.

The ideal relinquisher, filled with sattva and clear of doubt, neither resents unpleasant work nor clings to pleasant work. Tyaga, relinquishment, here means letting go of likes and dislikes about action, not giving up action itself. The next verse explains why.

No embodied being can give up action entirely, Krishna says. So the true tyagi, the relinquisher, is the one who gives up the fruit of action. This is the heart of his answer to the question Arjuna asked at the start of the chapter.

Knowledge, action and the doer are each threefold by the gunas. Sattvic knowledge sees one imperishable reality in all beings, undivided among the divided. Advaita reads it as the one Self in all; other schools, as the same divine presence or the same kind of self in every being.

posts.display: But that knowledge which regardeth the several manifold existences in all beings as separate, that knowledge know thou as of passion.
posts.caption: Rajasic knowledge sees only separateness: many different beings, each apart from the others. It notices the differences between things and misses what the previous verse called the undivided reality within them.

Tamasic knowledge clings to one small thing as if it were everything, without reason or real grasp of truth. Together these three verses trace a movement from narrow fixation, through seeing the many, to seeing the one.

Action, too, has three kinds. Sattvic action is what is required, done without attachment, without craving or aversion, by someone who does not seek its fruit. It is the Gita's karma yoga summed up in a single verse.

The sattvic doer is free of attachment and ego, full of steadiness and enthusiasm, and unchanged by success or failure. That evenness in success and failure recalls 2:48, where Krishna defines yoga itself as evenness of mind.

The tamasic doer, ruled by inertia, is undisciplined, coarse, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent and procrastinating. Where the sattvic doer works steadily and the rajasic doer works from greed, this list paints someone whose work is careless, grudging and endlessly put off. The Sanskrit for procrastinating, dirgha-sutri, literally means one who makes a long thread, stretching a task out without end.

Next Krishna sorts understanding by the gunas. Buddhi, the discerning intellect (Besant's "Reason"), is sattvic when it knows when to act and when to refrain, what to fear and what not, what binds and what frees. In plain terms, a clear mind can tell what is right to do. The rajasic kind confuses right and wrong, and the tamasic kind, wrapped in darkness, takes wrong for right.

Krishna sorts willpower, too, by the three gunas. Dhriti, steadfastness or resolve, is sattvic when through yoga it holds the mind, breath and senses steady without wavering. The rajasic kind holds on to duty, pleasure and wealth for the sake of reward; the tamasic kind cannot let go of sleep, fear, grief and conceit. The point is that determination is only as good as what it serves.

Happiness, too, has three kinds. Sattvic happiness is like poison at first and nectar in the end, and it arises from a clear understanding of the Self. The bitterness at the start is usually read as the effort of discipline, the sweetness as the peace that grows from it.

Rajasic happiness reverses the pattern: it comes from the senses meeting their objects, sweet as nectar at first and like poison in the end. Tamasic happiness, the next verse says, deludes from start to finish and comes from sleep, laziness and carelessness.

Krishna turns to the culmination of the path. One whose mind is unattached everywhere, self-mastered and free of craving reaches, through renunciation, the highest perfection of naishkarmya, freedom from action's bonds. Commentators differ on the details, but the core idea is a state in which action no longer binds a person at all. Shankara's disciple Sureshvara named a treatise after it, Naishkarmya Siddhi.

One who has become Brahman (brahma-bhuta) is serene, neither grieving nor craving, equal toward all beings, and so gains the highest devotion to Krishna. Shankara reads it as devotion marked by knowledge, the jnani's devotion of 7:16-17; Vaishnava teachers read it as loving devotion that realization opens into.

Through bhakti, Krishna says, the devotee knows him as he truly is, and knowing him, enters into him. Advaita reads that entering as union with Brahman; Vaishnava schools read it as coming into God's presence while remaining distinct.

Even while performing all actions, one who takes refuge in Krishna reaches the eternal, imperishable state through his grace, prasada. The active life and the goal of liberation are not set against each other. Grace recurs in the verses that follow.

The Lord, ishvara, dwells in the heart of every being, turning all creatures by his maya, his power. Besant renders the image as a potter's wheel; the Sanskrit yantra can mean any device or mechanism. Some commentators picture wooden figures moved by a mechanism, like puppets.

In the verse before, Krishna speaks of the Lord who dwells in the heart of every being. Here he urges Arjuna to take refuge in that Lord with his whole being, and promises supreme peace and the eternal abode through the Lord's grace. Shanti, peace, is one of the Gita's recurring words for the goal.

Having given his teaching, Krishna does not simply command. He tells Arjuna to reflect on it fully and then do as he chooses. Many readers see this as respect for Arjuna's own judgment, just before Krishna's final and most intimate words.

Krishna has called his teaching secret; now he offers his supreme word, the most secret of all. The reason he gives is personal: Arjuna is dear to him. The two verses that follow, a call to devotion and to surrender, are among the best-loved lines of the Gita.

One of the most discussed verses in the Gita. Krishna tells Arjuna to give up all dharmas (Besant's "duties") and take refuge in him alone, promising to free him from all sins: "sorrow not." Sri Vaishnavas call it the charama shloka, the ultimate verse, the basis of their teaching of prapatti, surrender to God. Shankara reads it as renouncing all works for knowledge of the one Self.

Krishna says that whoever studies this sacred dialogue worships him through jnana-yajna, the sacrifice of knowledge. The idea goes back to chapter 4, which ranks the offering of knowledge above material offerings. Study itself becomes a form of worship.

With the teaching complete, Krishna asks Arjuna two questions: has he listened with a focused mind, and has his delusion, born of ignorance, been destroyed? The dialogue comes back to where it began, with Arjuna's confusion in chapters 1 and 2.

Arjuna's answer, his last words in the Gita. His delusion is gone, his doubts are dispelled, and he will act on Krishna's word. Besant has "knowledge" for what he regains, but the Sanskrit smriti means memory, often read as remembering his true nature.

Sanjaya, narrating to the blind king Dhritarashtra, speaks again. The sage Vyasa, traditionally the author of the Mahabharata, had given him divine sight to see and hear the battlefield from afar. Through that gift, he says, he heard this yoga from Krishna himself.

Remembering the wondrous dialogue between Krishna, here called Keshava, and Arjuna, Sanjaya rejoices again and again. The doubled Sanskrit word, samsmritya samsmritya, gives the line a rhythm of joy that keeps returning.

The Gita's final verse. Sanjaya declares that wherever Krishna, Lord of Yoga, and Arjuna, the archer, stand together, there are fortune, victory and well-being. With it this plan ends, and so does our walk through all eighteen chapters. Thank you for reading along.
